steps.text: This alert about lsass.exe writing a registry value under a path containing '\RunTime\' looks like a likely false positive triggered by matching the "\Run" substring rather than an actual autorun key — I should check the relation to confirm.

arguments.reasoning: See the registry path and value lsass wrote.
Get the full registry key path to see whether it is a Run autostart key.
Verify lsass.exe image path and parent.

steps.text: This is actually benign — W32Time SecureTimeLimits is a standard Secure Time Seeding value updated by lsass, and the detection just false-matched "\Run" within "\RunTime\". I'll submit this as benign.

submission.reasoning: False positive. At 04:16:27Z on workstation5, lsass.exe (C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe, the normal system path) wrote a QWORD tick-count value to HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\SecureTimeLimits\RunTime\SecureTimeTickCount. This key belongs to the Windows Time service's Secure Time Seeding feature, and Windows updates it routinely. It is not an autostart Run key. The rule fired only because the text '\Run' appears inside '\RunTime\'. The data written is a timestamp-style QWORD, not a command or a path to a program, so nothing was set up to run at startup.
